lee-057ac5: For the turbulent racket of First Man's 'tin can' capsule, Lee and Mildred Iatrou Morgan recorded the shakes and vibrations of motion-simulator rides, adding metallic stress and strain performed by Foley walkers Dan O'Connell and John Cucci.
lee-9175a4: In Barbie, Lee's team used vocal sounds throughout Barbieland, like a person playing with dolls: a refreshing female 'ahh' added when the fridge opens, beatbox layers in a Kens fight, airy vocal swishes as Ken flies. The Kens' plane was spinner fireworks pitched down.
lee-f2c33b: For La La Land’s freeway opening, Lee built the traffic-jam soundscape in stages: a few horns here and there that grow in number, then idling cars, then car radios playing a diverse mix of music, building into a cacophony that leads into the musical number.
previty-d8d082: In God of War Ragnarök, Previty sidechains ambience to the music's RMS, an idea he credits to supervisor Michael Kent: with very slow attack and release, as the score swells the ambience drops and gets a high-shelf cut, keeping its body but losing detail that fights the notes. Combat states duck it further.
previty-51c8bb: Previty gives every cinematic in God of War Ragnarök its own custom ambience mix state, because much of what plays under cutscenes is the live in-game ambience. With the game’s single unbroken camera, a hard ambience change at a transition would break immersion.
previty-c91b35: Previty on God of War Ragnarök’s eight-enemy fights: to stop them turning to mush, a per-frame system sorts enemies by threat: at most two sit in the high-priority bucket, while the rest are turned down and allowed to duck harder. You hear whoever is attacking you right now.
previty-885615: Previty explains that God of War Ragnarök scales its multiband sidechaining to overall game loudness: in a quiet cavern the ambience never pumps, but the louder the game gets, the harder the real-time side chains work to clear space for story dialogue.
nelson-046fd2: Nelson’s build order is strict: clean and clarify all dialogue first, shape the music around it, then add effects, then rebalance once everything is up. Layering lets him judge each component’s place.
nelson-646f5c: Nelson refuses to edit at the console: a dialogue editor and a music editor sit beside him so mixing stays mixing, and he commits EQ in hard dialogue premixes rather than virtual ones.
nelson-67dcdc: In Les Misérables, Nelson let effects fade away as each song began, often replaced by an orchestral bed, then creep back as the song ended to stitch the number into the next scene.
nelson-bb9265: At the Mille Miglia start in Ferrari, after cheering crowds, revving engines and Enzo’s pep talks, Nelson takes the track very quiet as Enzo walks away from the last driver, putting the audience inside his head.
behlmer-8b96fc: On the found-footage Cloverfield, Behlmer left effects largely unfiltered for impact while the dialogue was filtered and placed spatially to sell the feeling of standing behind the camera.
behlmer-441447: On Cloverfield, Behlmer avoided overdoing camera-handling sounds, using them only on deliberate camera moves or when the camera fell to the ground; some camera effects were recorded in quad, which gave them an enhanced sense of realism.
behlmer-49078f: Behlmer's first temp-mix pass on World War Z was quick and reactionary, like throwing paint at the wall; with its slow-motion moments in mind, where sound could carry the film, the team mapped out areas and established moments that it kept into the final mix.
jimenez-b64a43: Jimenez built Garm, the largest creature in God of War Ragnarök, for 3D audio: footstep sounds are tagged to each of the four paws and other sounds fire from points along his physics-driven chain, so walking underneath him puts sound all around the player.
jimenez-ec0320: Jimenez kept Ingrid, the talking sword in God of War Ragnarök, organic rather than digital: glass particles scattered on a bowed cymbal, recorded with a Sanken and slowed down for magic tinkle, plus ocarina and human whistles morphed together in Logic’s Alchemy to form her ‘voice’.
burtt-a25dc4: Burtt describes how, to record Lincoln’s own pocket watch, wound for perhaps the first time in a century at the Kentucky Historical Society, Greg Smith built a small soundproof box holding the watch and a tiny Tram lavalier mic, closing the lid to isolate its ticking.
minto-8b4106: Wind alone didn’t make Star Wars Battlefront’s Hoth feel right, so Minto’s team layered in howling wapiti elk, a door creaking in a storm and the interior of a cave behind a frozen waterfall.
minto-fca6b0: On Battlefield 4, Minto’s team at DICE took player Foley out of the HDR mix system so huge explosions could no longer cull your own footsteps, keeping a constant link between your character and the world.
jerden-a0ed23: Jerden’s trailer hierarchy: lock the music first, then fight for clean, intelligible dialogue (one of the hardest jobs in trailer audio), then shape the sound design around both.
jerden-9b6f17: Jerden builds one palette of sounds for a whole trailer campaign, from first teaser to featurettes, since some campaigns run to 15 trailers needing a consistent style; separately, he keeps favourite processing chains as saved templates and Soundminer racks, and stacks processes in Patchwork.
deenen-127683: For the Star Wars Battlefront trailer, Deenen’s team auditioned in-game effects against the trailer music; anything that couldn’t survive the pacing was redesigned, while the iconic franchise sounds stayed untouched.
deenen-e2f72d: For Need for Speed crash recordings, Deenen's team hired a crane to drop cars from 100 feet, and on every drop stuck an SM57 in the middle of the crash at the impact point, expecting it to die. After 40+ drops it had only a minor scratch.
deenen-636e77: Deenen’s 100-whooshes method: fill 10–20 tracks with long continuous material, bus it to a few submixes loaded with Doppler, flangers and envelope filters, sidechain-duck the buses against each other, gate in hits at the peaks, then ride faders live and record take after take.
deenen-e10883: A practice drill Deenen recommends: rebuild a favourite sound using only five random library sounds, one per category, for several days running. To reverse-engineer a reference, study each frequency band and play it at half or quarter speed.
deenen-9a2c32: Deenen's 'bigganizing' trick (Dave Farmer's term) for explosions and gunshots: gain-clip a sound by 20 dB, then run it through the decrackle function of a declicker. It gives a perception of distortion that feels big and powerful without actual distortion.
deenen-a68fb1: On Need for Speed: Most Wanted, Deenen's team recorded the cars without turbos so turbos could be added later for upgrades, and recorded each car on the road to capture the real shift mechanism, with the grunts, sputters and odd noises cars make while shifting.
deenen-a07824: Deenen describes how, for the Star Wars Battlefront trailers, his team took famous sounds from the original films, split out the tonal and noise layers, kept the tonal layers and added higher-fidelity noise layers, giving them control in a dense mix.
jenkins-b18ab9: On Mad Max: Fury Road, Jenkins kept Furiosa’s and Max’s dialogue in the centre speaker, while secondary characters were panned slightly toward where they sat in John Seale’s frame: if one of the wives sat to Max’s left, her dialogue was panned that way.
jenkins-3543a1: Jenkins on dialogue editor Kira Roessler’s work on Mad Max: Fury Road: she rebuilt small performance details such as Charlize Theron’s breathing so the all-ADR track carried the intimacy of production sound.
boyes-243bb7: For Avatar's 3D mix, Boyes's team moved only specific elements, such as a passing bullet Cameron singled out, from the back to the front, keeping copious notes of frame counts; Boyes says too much sonic information at once would detract from the experience.
scarabosio-3f1e6e: For the President’s speech in Don’t Look Up, Scarabosio’s team recorded the lines played through different TVs and speakers in different environments to build location-specific treatments.
scarabosio-ed2e92: Scarabosio gave speakers at Don’t Look Up’s naval event boosted low end and subtle distortion, as if the PA were overloading, so they sounded like they were overselling it.
anderson-06e42c: On Restrepo, Anderson's team used nature in the quiet moments so the world carries on serenely, then suddenly the chaos and distortion of violence. Ambiences, cut by Matt Snedecor, also showed where shots came from or went to, and where each soldier was.
hiland-be014c: In The Midnight Sky’s plane scene, Hiland’s team started big and wide outside, then pulled sound back as Augustine climbed in, so the audience had to lean in. Backgrounds were taken down and out to almost nothing until the gunshot brings the scene back.
hiland-8d5c1c: When blood appears in the astronaut’s helmet in The Midnight Sky, Hiland’s team slowly faded out every ship hum and exterior sound until only her breathing inside the helmet was left, making the moment claustrophobic.
dupre-49676c: Dupre mixed WandaVision's first episodes in mono, everything stacked in the center. Only subtle hints of a world outside the sitcom spread into stereo, until the shift to color opened the mix into the surrounds.
whitehead-9fc396: For District 9, Whitehead’s crew bred flies in the studio, then released them into the ADR room at Park Road Post to record swarm ambiences, single fly-bys and close group buzzing.
whitehead-e7a005: Whitehead’s finished prawn voices in District 9 are only about ten percent human. Consonant and vowel layers were premixed separately, with the consonants weighted heavier to push an insect-like quality, and rapid purring clicks act as the aliens’ ‘hmmm’ while thinking.
whitehead-113978: Whitehead built District 9’s Exo Suit from very lo-tech elements: typewriters, small appliance servos, dirt hits and steam-train chugs. He cut the first full version, then handed it to effects editor Hayden Collow for the final hard-effects sweetening pass before the mix.
whitehead-90555c: Whitehead on District 9: it was decided early that the lo-fi treatment of the security-camera footage would be done on the mix stage by re-recording mixers Mike Hedges and Gilbert Lake, so they could control the amount and type of futz used in the final.
acord-83f4b3: In Andor, Acord treated rebel comms as traditional, even futzy, radio, while the Imperial comm room used real and synthesized shortwave-like sounds for a WW2-era feel.
acord-d1f1bf: For The Mandalorian and Grogu, Acord’s team did a whole separate mix for home viewing, a near-field pass, taking care not to overcrowd the soundscape.
acord-939731: Acord’s Orbak grunts for The Rise of Skywalker are about 90% pitched, slowed-down crow, with a little donkey mixed in.
aadahl-e798b0: Aadahl's tank sound for The Creator came from veering his car into the serrated median of Highway 395; the whole car howled and he pulled over to record it. With tremolo it became the tank, and Malte Bieler lined up deep metallic clunks to its rhythm for close-ups.
aadahl-ec0aeb: Aadahl ran The Creator’s robot voices through digital vocoders controlled over MIDI, kept as live processing all the way through the final mix so treatments could still be adjusted on the stage.
aadahl-b3b3e7: For Godzilla, Aadahl’s team recorded with a Sanken CO-100K, which captures up to 100 kHz, then slowed the ultrasonic content down into hearing range—mining an ‘invisible universe’ for new textures.
aadahl-9d8ad4: In The Creator, as Alphie uses her power on the bomb robot, Aadahl's team took out the battle sounds to go internal, and chose not to base her power on a synthetic, computer-created sound, using an Aboriginal didgeridoo for its spiritual quality.
aadahl-1e3905: Aadahl found that in an anechoic chamber your ears tune in to your own circulation and breathing, so small sounds become really big. On A Quiet Place, that idea shaped Regan's sonic perspective, built on the chamber's isolation and emphasis on bodily noise.
ryn-7a4360: A Quiet Place’s creature clicks avoided real echolocating animals, which sounded too familiar; instead Van der Ryn’s team zapped grapes with a stun gun, standing in for flesh, and slowed the zaps down.
ryn-169847: To ‘world-ize’ Godzilla, Van der Ryn’s team blasted processed roars through a big speaker array on the Warner Bros. backlot and re-recorded them from rooftops and inside cars, capturing real urban echo.
ryn-86fd06: In A Quiet Place, director John Krasinski envisioned a low rumble for Regan's cochlear implant, which Van der Ryn calls 'hearing as touch'. In the three moments she removes the implant, Van der Ryn and Erik Aadahl used actual silence, digital zero, to connect the audience to her.
battaglia-291e05: Battaglia describes how the buzzing lights in Backrooms were recorded by Umberto Corte using electromagnetic and contact mics, capturing tones and textures in the fixtures that you would not normally hear with a conventional microphone.
battaglia-0e80c9: On Backrooms Battaglia’s team found the creature scarier through incidental sounds than through screams. A peg-leg footstep became the signature danger sound, sprinkled around the space and heard progressively clearer as the film goes on.
rydstrom-54b66f: West Side Story starts with a feeling of demolition, and Rydstrom's sound carries it on: in later scenes you hear the city being demolished off screen.
rydstrom-8656b1: In West Side Story's knife fight, Rydstrom kept the knife swishes realistic but scary and avoided high-pitched background sounds such as a sodium-vapor buzz, which would have hurt the swish of the knives.
rydstrom-722de2: To get from the rumble’s deaths to the upbeat ‘I Feel Pretty’ in West Side Story, Rydstrom’s team stripped away natural sound and left only church bells, giving the audience a moment to absorb the loss.
rydstrom-8db134: On Ad Astra, Rydstrom's team built many of the sounds heard early in the film from dialogue by Tommy Lee Jones and Liv Tyler taken from later scenes, looping them and transitioning them into music and soundscape, so you hear Jones long before you see him.
summers-0407a3: Avatar was mixed in 2D, so the mixers, Summers among them, watched each reel in 3D with James Cameron, silent and close to the screen. Cameron called out what came off the screen, and they carried that spatial memory back to the stage to make sure those sounds came through.
summers-d1d8c4: Summers recalls that in Avatar’s thanator chase, James Cameron stopped the mix because he couldn’t hear Jake breathing under the roars and the music. Keeping the hero’s panicked breath audible kept the scene about the character rather than just a big monster sequence.
whittle-d91d45: Yates Whittle notes that Cameron places sounds in the spaces between dialogue, not over it. In Fire and Ash’s forest scene each brush hit was timed to both the action and the lines: nothing haphazard.
whittle-68135f: To check Kiri’s voice on Avatar: The Way of Water, Yates Whittle compared Sigourney Weaver’s recordings with clips of deep-voiced 14- and 15-year-old girls. Pitch changes were minimal, a quarter to half semitone on a few syllables, and some lines were untouched.
whittle-923b96: Yates Whittle describes how, in Fire and Ash’s ‘Miracle’ scene, the score arrived early so effects could carve out frequency space for it, and Spider’s breathing was shaped to grow shallower and less frequent, building anticipation with the music.
whittle-22704a: Kevin Dorman’s voice is inside the Tulkun vocals in Avatar: Fire and Ash but processed to remove its human quality, because, Yates Whittle notes, the human voice is something you can always pick out.
whittle-227220: Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol had loads of Russian dialogue shot with Czech actors. Yates Whittle had St. Petersburg-born Skywalker colleague Mika Makarov watch the whole film flagging accents and wrong phrasing for replacement, then brought him to Tom Cruise’s ADR sessions to coach his Russian.
whittle-33ea57: On Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol's Burj Khalifa climb, Yates Whittle's team kept production breaths and efforts, usually the first things lost. Scenes not shot with IMAX cameras, like the hotel room, were recorded cleanly enough that much production dialogue survived.
whittle-2e8075: Tron: Legacy’s light-up suits put a whine on all the production dialogue. Yates Whittle’s team cut it clean first, sent it for specialised spectral noise removal, then ran cleanup passes at the premix and again at the final, rescuing most of the production.
ribicoff-07208b: Severance opens with ordinary fluorescent and computer hums in Lumon’s halls; Ribicoff introduces the stretched-breath room tones gradually as the story turns stranger, and layering them in and out keeps long corridor tracking shots from going static.
ribicoff-f6dd71: In Severance's Break Room scenes, a reversed speech that came from the picture department plays so low it hides behind the dialogue. Ribicoff's team enhanced how it sat in the room, making it a shadowy, muffled voice from somewhere indirect.
jennings-b779de: For A Minecraft Movie’s ‘First Night’ sequence, Jennings pitched a version without temp music, letting sound design be the score: familiar game sounds like skeleton bone clinks and zombie moans, an accelerating heartbeat as the pulse, building to a brief pause before a volley of flaming arrows is launched.
jennings-1ab7da: In A Minecraft Movie, sound design stepped back for Jack Black’s songs. For Garrett’s ‘When I’m Gone’ introduction, where music and design played as equals, Jennings worked in lockstep with music editor Jamieson Shaw using tempo maps, sync points and tuned sound effects as the music changed at least five times.
rohde-2d04a6: Rohde notes that Imagineering sends mixed teams on field research: architects, writers, set designers, fabricators. Each discipline notices different things, so a group corrects the blind spots any one observer brings home.
rohde-0671a6: Rohde says every executive review of Animal Kingdom began with the park’s themes restated before any idea was shown. Reviewers judged each proposal against agreed principles, not personal taste.
lanier-1c05bc: Lanier describes how The Last of Us used an in-house ‘stochastic obstruction’ system: every game frame it threw out roughly 1,500 to 2,500 random raycasts purely for audio, spending a real chunk of the PS3’s Cell processor to model how walls and objects occlude sounds in its environments.
slater-a61866: Baby Driver opens with the studio logo re-pitched by Slater so its ping rings out into an infinite reverb tail that becomes tinnitus, in the same key as the strings that follow; a car’s brake squeal, reverse-echoed in that key, then leads into the first song.
oconnell-590e5f: O’Connell treats the temp mix as a pre-final: in his estimate 80–90 percent of a film’s sonic blueprint gets locked during the temp process, so it deserves real care.
oconnell-cc4ff5: O’Connell explains that on Transformers the Autobots were pitched down about a semitone and Decepticons two or three, played through a small speaker in a chamber, then blended with the dry track for edge.
ribicoff-746bcf: For Helly’s backstage moment in Severance, Ribicoff pitch-bent crowd recordings, panned them in a full circle around the room following the camera, and rode them in surges, creating a seasick disorientation.
jennings-426c5f: Jennings describes Dave Whitehead’s trick on A Minecraft Movie: worldizing existing sounds with transducers that vibrate the objects they’re attached to. A palette of vocal phrases for the Iron Golem, OK on its own, took on new life once played through metal I-beams and sheets of diamond plate.
jennings-083414: For A Minecraft Movie, Jennings’s team built the Orb of Dominance palette from glass objects: his wedding ring spun furiously inside a vase until it shattered, a metal spoon rubbed inside a cube-shaped candle holder, and a transducer playing bubbling water against an empty drinking glass.
foscato-b7baac: For WandaVision’s finale crowd, Foscato’s team went through three or four loop-group recording passes as the cut evolved. The first passes were too big and angry. The final version layered many subtle choking sounds and heavy breathing into a pad that didn’t intrude.
patrick-04a517: For Redwing’s chirps in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Patrick played small ceramic water-filled bird whistles as if ‘talking’, then ran them through Soundtoys Crystallizer presets, giving beeps that still hint at a bird. Nia Hansen had suggested Crystallizer for widening sources.
gilmore-f66783: For the research-ship crash in Alien: Earth, every member of Gilmore’s team tried complex layered passes on the thrusters that keep firing once the ship is lodged in a building. What worked in the end was a few chopped-up rocket recordings. Gilmore’s point: pick one cool sound, not ten.
gilmore-b24d1a: On Alien: Earth, no Xenomorph close-up got a single stock scream. Gilmore’s team rebuilt every appearance from base layers, with performances that ramp from something like a simmering tea kettle into a hero scream, so the creature reads as angry, plotting or toying with its prey.
gilmore-043797: Gilmore’s team laid Alien: Earth lab backgrounds as room tone first, then dressed them with spotted call-and-response machines. In the transfer room, where Marcy feels safe, the backgrounds are slightly discordant to suggest something isn’t right.
shatz-972c99: On Milk, Felix Andrew used a stereo M/S mic as the primary boom; in the mix Shatz put the lav in the center and the M/S on the sides, calibrating M/S-to-mono and spread. M/S scenes needed M/S ADR, so he faked room color with TL Space reverb.
hirschberg-0cb685: In World War Z Hirschberg removed the percussion the audience expected; with the drums gone, viewers’ own heartbeats supplied the tension and Anna Behlmer’s effects had room to land.
stoeckinger-443abd: In John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum’s glass-room fight, Stoeckinger’s team gave each weapon set its own sound, altering mostly library sources: bludgeoning first, then small blades with higher, faster swishes and shings, then samurai swords with more power, more low end and lower-pitched swipes.
stoeckinger-54843b: Stoeckinger’s team can stack 12 to 15 sounds on a single John Wick headshot, and every gunshot carries a faint layer of mechanism — detail audiences never consciously notice but would miss immediately if it were stripped out.
stoeckinger-bc3db1: Stoeckinger’s old-school trick for rapid fire: leave a blank frame between consecutive gunshots so each one starts with a clean attack instead of smearing into the tail of the last.
stoeckinger-09d4bb: Wick is always grabbing someone else’s gun, so when a villain’s weapon lands in his hands Stoeckinger’s team can add extra low end and size to it — the sound follows the character, not just the prop.
andersen-308fc5: For Control's supernatural Hiss, which needed a real-world reference yet sounded unfamiliar, Andersen went to Paris and recorded weird organic textures with Nicolas Becker, such as a friction mallet rubbed against the enclosure of an EMT plate reverb.
andersen-ced7e8: On Inside, Andersen's team sampled a 1980s flagship Roland R-880 hardware reverb and used it as the in-game environmental reverb via convolution; its glossy, gritty low-resolution sound worked for both environments and music, so the music's reverb changes with the space you're in.
andersen-ed5481: Andersen ran all of Limbo's sounds through an old tape recorder, which made them sit well together in the mix. His own physics recordings sounded too real, so he put them through an old spring reverb set to zero, using it as a hardware filter that thinned them until they became generic.
andersen-2a7a39: Andersen structured Limbo’s soundscape as a journey: it starts as fairly naturalistic forest and grows steadily more abstract, almost transcendent, as the game progresses.
andersen-82b6cc: Andersen’s team on Inside put a wired contact mic into a professional sword swallower’s stomach, recording internal body ambience and projecting sounds into it; a captured heartbeat became the metronome for the lineup puzzle.
wood-71930a: Wood on Kylo Ren’s mask voice: it was built in sound design first, then handed to Adam Driver to perform through. Because the processing responded to his delivery in real time, he could get up on the mic and play it like an instrument.
wood-85cd68: Wood on BB-8: it was voiced through a tactile interface that let the performer change timbre and pitch by hand. Ben Schwartz’s recordings acted as an English placeholder telling Wood’s team what BB-8 was feeling and saying.
semanick-aa48ed: In Incredibles 2’s newscast that follows the signal down the wire, Semanick passed the voice through different futzes for the broadcast booth, added static over radio waves, and room reverb that filled then narrowed as the camera moved, with splits on everything.
morgan-5606ab: On First Man, where original Mission Control recordings had to match the actors' dialogue, Iatrou Morgan kept every line clear enough to understand but left in a lot of texture and fuzz, keeping the dialogue unpolished like a documentary.
morgan-30e251: On La La Land, Iatrou Morgan and mixer Andy Nelson kept noisy production dialogue to anchor the film in reality, sometimes patching just a word or syllable with ADR. For the hilltop duet she built a background fill of the noisy dialogue background and carried it into the song.
morgan-405bdf: Iatrou Morgan notes that because La La Land’s production mixer kept the actors miked even during playback takes, there was always usable live material — the roommates’ on-set gasps and little shrieks ended up in their musical number.
becker-9853a7: Becker on Sound of Metal: its deafening silences are a matter of dynamics. The opening concert is so loud and strong that it sets the film’s general level and paves the way for experiencing silence later, like repeatedly hitting your hand with a hammer, then stopping and feeling sudden relief.
menichini-b72377: Menichini’s team mixed the Overwatch trailer in Atmos around the camera’s point of view, so a sniper firing from off-screen could be heard behind and above the audience rather than just in the surrounds.
menichini-9abd9d: One element in Reaper's Death Blossom bullet-bys in the Overwatch trailer, Menichini says, was a series of processed pig dopplers that Charles Deenen had created some time before and gave the team to use.
ottosson-cfeaf2: For 2012’s destruction library Ottosson spent days recording rocks and ruptures on a Foley stage, printed them to analog tape, then varispeeded and re-recorded into the DAW at 192 kHz for further mangling.
ottosson-be5291: On 2012, Ottosson wanted the destruction to sound interesting and huge without having to be played very loud. He used multiband compression so a sound bites where it needs to and is held back where it hurts, without sucking the life out of it.
ottosson-46807f: In 2012’s action, something nearly always pre-laps the picture cut by five to seven frames; in slower scenes the pre-lap might run for seconds, but Ottosson tries to justify each one with something on screen.
ottosson-0a5b29: A continuous built rumble underpinned 2012’s earthquake chase so sudden impacts had something to punch out of. Ottosson built almost all the sub content himself, using a sub harmonizer only for water.
ottosson-5c1fdf: On The Hurt Locker, Ottosson mixed gun attacks through compressors to get each weapon's kick, sometimes compressing and pushing the swell of the shot echoing around the mountains, and mixed the tails after each shot with their own EQ and compression.
ottosson-40a6a7: Inside the bomb suit in The Hurt Locker, Ottosson let the technician's breathing carry the scene, so we get his mindset; Kathryn Bigelow liked it as an astronaut walking alone in space. He played the breath all around the room, even when the camera was close.
ottosson-1781a8: To build tension on The Hurt Locker, Ottosson would start with a real environment sound and morph it into something a bit strange, still real but strange; he felt audiences didn't hear the change but sensed something unnatural.
ottosson-053860: On The Hurt Locker, Ottosson broke the centre-channel convention, panning dialogue and Foley with the action in chaotic scenes, then filled every side with backgrounds so no speaker felt empty. Even simple backgrounds got fader rides and EQ sweeps.
albrechtsen-4434eb: Albrechtsen describes how, for animated sequences of experiments with human cells in the documentary The Immortalists, recordist Mikkel Nielsen placed a mic inside a dead fish to get proper internal-organ sounds, partly because the animations had an underwater feel.
albrechtsen-0aa418: Albrechtsen uses total silence in pretty much every film, because a movie can have the complete silence no real place has. In The Killing of Two Lovers, Freeland and We Are As Gods, the most emotionally powerful moments for him were moments of total silence.
albrechtsen-bd885c: In The Last Race, a stock-car sequence plays against Mozart, so Albrechtsen built the car sounds to the music: crashes land on string swells, and skids and tyre screeches are pitched in the same tone as the music.
albrechtsen-7e84e0: Wanting something weightier than a stock whoosh for a flying witch, Albrechtsen pitched down a recording of his old washing machine and added reverb. His library is tagged both by source and by what each sound evokes, which surfaces surprises.
thom-a5a9b6: Thom made the explosions in How to Train Your Dragon deliberately heavy in low frequencies. That let them feel powerful and shake the whole environment without being ear-piercingly loud, which they would have to be if the intensity came from mids and highs.
thom-c97ac7: Thom’s team used ‘virtual pre-mixing’ on How to Train Your Dragon: every candidate effect sat in sync in a Pro Tools session, uncommitted, until the final mix. Since the final score often arrives on day one of the final, the effects could still be reshaped to fit the music.
thom-6f5350: On The Midnight Sky spacewalk, Foley was recorded flat in case the director rejected the treatment, then muffled and made bass-heavy in post to suggest bone conduction. Thom admits the processing was simply a low-pass filter, and Thom’s team introduced the effect gently.
klyce-86eb00: In The Killer, metal is a sound theme tied to the character: guns, cars, storage units, license plates, and the fingerprint-resistant metal cup he drinks from, so Klyce's team had to design the cup touching other metal surfaces and even an airplane fold-down tray.
klyce-4eb543: On The Killer, Fincher and editor Kirk Baxter found voiceover worked best never heard in the character's POV shots. Klyce describes those POV shots getting their own sound, often loud Smiths music then sudden quiet, so effects and textures change dramatically on each perspective cut.
klyce-4eea2d: For Mank’s old-theatre echo, Klyce’s team moved from impulse responses to the real thing: they played the final mix back on Skywalker’s hard-walled Scoring Stage, captured it with a dozen mics spaced from screen to back wall, and blended that reverb into the rear surrounds.
klyce-8886d7: Klyce on The Social Network: the first mixes were conservative, with dialogue up and background and music suppressed. Fincher had the bar overtake the opening break-up and the Ruby Skye club music overpower the dialogue, leaving lines on the edge of intelligibility so the audience struggles to listen in.
beggs-c77acd: In Somewhere, Beggs made the two portentous low-frequency pulses as the Ferrari passes under viaducts from a manipulated bullwhip rush, and built the musical drone beneath the engine from multitrack elements of a song by Phoenix, the film’s band.
king-4b9cec: King’s team built Oppenheimer’s black-hole collapse from a reversed explosion swept hard with EQ and layered with crushing rock, giving the sense of an implosion that never ends.
king-31710b: King describes how, in Maestro's Ely Cathedral Mahler performance, the mixers gently pulled out all the backgrounds when the music kicked in and brought the world back only when it finished: a pregnant pause with the audience stunned, then the applause crashes in.
king-0dcf0c: King gave each Oppenheimer location its own character: Los Alamos uses wind, rain, thunder and wildlife to accentuate distance, such as a bird call or coyote howl placed far away with a lot of reverb, while the oppressive Gray Commission hearing room gets a low, airy rumble.
king-9141bf: In Oppenheimer, the sound of stamping feet is a motif Nolan wanted used several times before the bomb is dropped, growing louder and more oppressive. King describes it as a device to convey Oppenheimer’s growing panic about what the creation of the weapon meant to the world.
king-80c15f: King’s team didn’t match Inception’s slow-motion shots with slowed sound: they either ignored the speed change entirely or played sounds unrelated to the action.
king-e8d534: At Nolan’s suggestion, King’s team shifts the pitch of real-world sounds in Inception as the dreamers drop a level, so the roar inside a jet morphs into city traffic on entering the first dream.
king-1281bf: For Oppenheimer’s Trinity test, King drew on eyewitness accounts from physicists stationed at different distances, each describing it differently: a very sharp bang with a long decay, like thunder rumbling around the surrounding hills. The bunker and everything in it shakes when the shock wave hits.
king-cc49f3: For Dunkirk's Stuka siren, King built an electric-driven siren inside a 30-gallon steel drum with clamped resonators and recorded it in the desert, where it ricocheted around the hills. In the studio he added natural distortion, as if the sound were ripping through the air.
king-8e245b: For Dunkirk's trawler target-practice scene, King's team shot pieces of metal standing in for the hull, with a suppressor on the gun so only the impacts were heard. Nolan designed the scene so the hits land in pregnant pauses, scaring the audience like the soldiers inside.
king-aa5754: Bane’s mask hid Tom Hardy’s mouth, so King’s team on The Dark Knight Rises exaggerated the clarity of his voice. Early experiments added fluid through tubes, breathing and gaseous layers, but they made him harder to understand, so King’s team stripped them out and kept the voice largely natural.
king-363a81: King on Interstellar: Nolan wanted production dialogue with almost no looping, only six to eight lines. Dialogue editors Hugo Weng and Bob Kaiser cut it like sound effects, dropping in syllables from other takes to articulate words better.
king-ff0b24: King describes how Interstellar’s violent launch buffets needed character beyond a dropped aircraft wing, so Ken Johnson spent weeks recording a vibrating table loaded with metal to get layers of small rattles.
king-b899a8: King on Tenet’s highway chase: the cars, including a turbocharged BMW M5, were chosen partly for their sound. To sell the low camera angle, Eric Potter recorded small road details: bumps, lane changes, running onto the shoulder, a tyre hitting a manhole cover. Drifts and skids were recorded separately for processing.
king-389267: For Tenet’s inverted world, King kept literal reversal to a minimum. Wind was designed to feel like suction instead of gusts, and the seagulls were built to sound like an echo of real gulls. King’s team found early on that simply playing elements backwards didn’t feel strange or special enough.
king-ed1f1a: King’s team worldized much of Tenet. Fight blows, kicks and inverted explosions were played through a loudspeaker and re-recorded in corridors and rooms with interesting echo. King values the acoustic accidents this gives, which are hard to get from plugins.
bridgett-a5e81b: In Shadow of the Tomb Raider, Bridgett placed death whistles and conch horns from the score's FX stems off-screen in 3D with no explained source, preferring mid-distance to far because it makes players more uncomfortable; not knowing if a sound is score or real was the team's state of fear.
hein-423fec: In The United States vs. Billie Holiday, Hein's team prepped the early clubs with loop group and sound effects so the audience talks and yells over Billie, because she wasn't famous yet. As her fame rises, the audiences grow larger.
mills-bec12b: For Inside Out’s memory orbs, which needed to feel glassy but sweet and musical, Mills’s team recorded different glasses filled with varying volumes of water to find the right pitches, then pitched them up and down, which became the sound of memories rewinding.
hayes-ea9d94: On Les Misérables, Hayes’s lavs sat on the outside of costumes at the centre of the chest, disguised with costume offcuts glued over them and painted out with CGI where needed. That kept clothing rustle off the vocals.
lievsay-5df04c: Lievsay’s team built the I Am Legend creatures from recorded actors and animals, edited for hours into vocal types; temp mixes of each type for the director shaped how the creatures behaved and fed back into the CG design.
lievsay-6b26e8: Lievsay fully built the 20-second stillness after No Country’s car crash: far-off traffic, a distant dog, glass tinkling down at three separate moments. None of it came from a mic on set—each sound was chosen and placed.
lievsay-297654: Lievsay’s mix of Gravity panned every voice with its actor wherever they floated, focusing the eye but also disorienting the audience. For Atmos, the essentially mono dialogue became objects carrying the 7.1 pans, then tracked even more precisely with added height.
boeddeker-dc8ea3: On Black Panther, Boeddeker's team made Wakanda's technology sounds high-tech and a bit musical but rooted in something organic and African: the signature pass-by of some airships and trains was an African bird slowed way down, with Kontakt used for layering and pitch manipulation.
boeddeker-e25967: On Black Panther, Boeddeker split the Royal Talon Fighter into three jobs: air displacement whooshes for size and speed, pitched tonal propulsion, and mechanical fin movement to ground it. Propulsion came in two or three separable layers so one could be chosen to sit with the final score.
boeddeker-46bc2a: On Black Panther, early VFX made bullets look like ricochets off the Panther suit, but the intent was absorption. So Boeddeker reversed metallic hits and layered them with contact sounds, making rounds seem to thud into the suit and drop.
boeddeker-5c9da3: For Black Panther’s spirit-world scenes Boeddeker found an endlessly evolving Reaktor tone whose pitch sometimes harmonized with the score and sometimes drifted against it — beautiful but subtly unsettling.
boeddeker-200acc: In Black Panther’s waterfall challenge fights the falls had to feel powerful without exhausting ears, so Boeddeker pulled their presence back to let Foley, dialogue and many added effort sounds connect the audience to the fighters.
boeddeker-9bf7eb: On Black Panther, Boeddeker and Brandon Proctor shared the music faders: in dialogue-led scenes the dialogue mixer took the music and ducked it around lines, and where music and effects shared a frequency range, the effects mixer took the music so the two wouldn't fight.
bellemare-7a69a9: Bellemare’s team built Arrival’s alien logograms from Foley of vegetables and rice moving in water, plus metal brushes scraped across a plastic board — deliberately organic sources instead of an electronic sci-fi palette.
bellemare-98e078: For the subtle atmosphere around the alien shell in Arrival, Bellemare's team cut wind recordings really tight into tiny fragments and intercut them with fragments of a different kind of wind, so the pieces jump into each other; the result sits very low in the mix.
bellemare-adbcd0: In Arrival’s flashbacks, Bellemare’s team uses natural sound with no pitching or processing; instead sounds from the present bleed into the past and back, with gentle fader moves and light EQ tying the timelines together.
bellemare-a84a18: For Arrival's radios and comms, Bellemare's team re-recorded every line that passes through a device: a full-range speaker played the line into real transmitting devices, and the receivers' output, such as a baby monitor, was miked into Pro Tools instead of using Speakerphone or EQ.
bellemare-722cdd: In Arrival, a helicopter clashed with Jóhann Jóhannsson’s score in the same frequency band, so Bellemare’s team reshaped its pitch and harmonics until it threaded through the music while still reading as a helicopter.
nielsen-eeaddb: The Garthim in Age of Resistance had to echo the original film’s castanet-like clatter yet be new. Nielsen’s answer was a pinecone rolled around a wooden bowl, then pitched down.
prebble-00f59b: For 30 Days of Night’s vampire kills, Prebble used persimmon, rock melon and semi-dry seaweed, plus contact-mic recordings of shellfish being manipulated, aiming for real intent rather than stylized action.
prebble-482d6a: For 30 Days of Night, a linguist developed the vampires' language, voiced with an incursive technique on the in-breath, and Prebble's team cast performers including death-metal vocalists. Humans show cold breath on screen but vampires never do, so the team emphasized the in-breath's vocal power.
prebble-0111f6: Prebble's favorite sound scene in 30 Days of Night is one of its quietest: mixers Michael Hedges and Gethin Creagh slowly removed every real or normal element until near-silence, and by the climax all natural ambiences had been replaced by very subtle tones.
johnson-a50af4: On Alice in Wonderland, Johnson kept London sounding normal and rather bland, while Underland used strange birds, insects and frogs. Each place got its own sound: the White Queen's castle by waterfalls fuller and lusher than the Red Queen's, and the final battle area only stark, lonely wind.
johnson-e663d0: On Alice in Wonderland, Johnson left Alice's voice quality unchanged when she changed size, to avoid distracting from the performance. In the round room, her reverb was tight and small when she was big and larger and more alive when small; her big footsteps got deeper.
myers-4cb5c8: On Toy Story 3, Myers continued the conceit from working with Gary Rydstrom: when the toys interact with humans as inanimate objects, they sound smaller in scale than the human world, but walking and talking among themselves their sounds take on an almost human scale.
solis-58d3b5: At the peak of the loud LSD sequence in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Solis tried pulling a master fader all the way down as a test. Absolute silence worked better than the usual low drone or bed, and Solis’s team kept it.
solis-0e953b: Woman of the Hour’s opening was originally full of ambience. Tony Solis pared it back to near silence to teach the audience early that silence is intentional, not a QC error. When Rodney chases Sarah, Solis’s team dropped her distant screams entirely: seeing the struggle without hearing it feels more desolate.
hachisako-8b9074: Hachisako’s team calculated Resident Evil 7’s ambiences against how long players linger in a room: positioned wind, rattling windows and subtle unsettling horror tones build stress gradually, and stretches of silence are protected so players imagine what comes next.
files-e29fe2: For the facehugger corridor in Alien: Romulus, Files’s team had built complex creature vocals placed in Atmos at different reverb depths. When they muted all of it and kept only body movement and a few details, everyone agreed the scene was much better.
files-c29614: Files mixed Alien: Romulus with layers of film saturation and distortion under everything, and the opening near-silence carries film hiss, not digital zero. Silence in space is suggested by rolling off the high frequencies, which audiences accept as silence.
files-91bf0d: In The Invisible Man’s opening escape, Files’s team first played the waves loud to cover Cecilia’s sneaking, then reversed it: they pulled the waves out so she suddenly felt exposed. Files says nearly every mix decision followed her point of view.
files-9dbec2: For the camera-covered suit in The Invisible Man, Files’s team fed camera clicks and servos into the particle-based Sound Particles software, multiplied and randomised by the thousand, until it sounded almost insect-like. They used only tiny tastes of it when Cecilia senses something.
files-408de5: Files describes how, on The Invisible Man, P.K. Hooker ran room sounds such as a cricket through the invisible man’s suit-voice processing. When the camera settles on a spot, the faint warping hints that something stands between the sound and the lens.
stateman-b77dc5: For Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood, Stateman’s team recorded eight period cars in one day on a back road, with each recorder locked to one position and point of view — multichannel interiors, aggressive exteriors, onboard maneuvers — then spent six weeks mastering.
rohde-fef6d9: Rohde’s cinematographer father’s storyboards taught him that a drawing can be a plan. Creative work is not all spontaneity; much of it can be choreographed in advance.
lee-0e221e: In La La Land’s musical numbers, Lee cuts Foley to the music’s rhythm rather than strict sync, chooses its pitch and tone so it won’t clash with the score, and drops footsteps entirely where they’d fight the song.
nelson-e973fd: In Les Misérables, as Samantha Barks sings ‘On My Own’, Nelson painted in a gentle stereo rain, then quickly reduced it the moment she began because her live recording already had rain on it, slowly reintroducing a little stereo rain at the end before the next sequence.
sullivan-c099cb: In The Woman King's dance-battle sequence, Sullivan's team went meticulously into each production track to get the machete hits out of the dialogue and singing without hurting the performances, then augmented the scene with Foley.
minto-aad7ac: To recreate the original blasters for Star Wars Battlefront, Minto struck a guy-wire for its classic twang. For a new R-series droid voice, he recorded his baby son's cooing and processed it the way Ben Burtt processed R2-D2 in the original film.
deenen-dfb15b: For the Star Wars Battlefront trailer, rather than only reusing finished composite sounds, Deenen’s team recreated the elements that made them up. Having the parts let them build new movements and new points of view, aided by flangers, phasers and detuned speed playback.
scarabosio-d22c25: For the pods detaching in space in Don’t Look Up, Scarabosio had to find sounds in the low-mids without the high-end aspect; the comet-landing explosions got more tonality and low end than loud Earth explosions.
whitehead-0c6c45: Sea-mammal clicks didn’t read as language for District 9’s aliens, so Whitehead invented one with hundreds of words. He performed each alien line himself, then replaced the consonants with a custom palette and the vowels with treated animal and vegetable-rubbing sounds.
whitehead-d41c40: Before any animation existed for District 9, Whitehead built an alien-weapon palette from bees, pipe hits and blows, nail guns and synths through effects chains, then handed it to Brent Burge, who cut the final booming guns.
acord-465e6e: In The Force Awakens, Kylo Ren’s Force rumble is Acord’s cat’s purr, pitched, slowed down and given a ton of added low end.
acord-714906: Exegol in The Rise of Skywalker has constant lightning flashes, but Acord didn’t hit every one, which would exhaust the audience. He placed the scary lightning hits at peak-tension moments, sometimes waiting a couple of extra beats past the peak to catch viewers off guard.
acord-8d49f9: For Palpatine’s Force lightning blast at the fleet in The Rise of Skywalker, Abrams asked what it would sound like if it blew out the microphone. Acord’s root sound was an electric toothbrush on sheet metal, overdriven again and again with added low end, played as a big overhead Atmos moment.
farmer-823ffa: Farmer delights in casting a sound against type, as when a wet car pass-by became a flare gun firing in The Island of Dr. Moreau. If the audience never questions it, the repurposed source has done its job.
aadahl-67c4f5: For Argo, archival footage showed 1979 Tehran used European two-tone sirens. Aadahl’s team built a car rig with two pneumatic two-tone horns, police and ambulance, and recordist P.K. Hooker drove it around the Warner Bros. lot to capture both close-ups and distant-city siren perspectives.
ryn-bb7940: On A Quiet Place Part II, as on the first film, Van der Ryn and Aadahl skipped the usual spotting session with Krasinski: they spent a couple of days alone with the cut, reacting instinctively, then sent him a scene or two for feedback so he had something real to react to.
gearty-0d2f03: Recording nine period cars at Floyd Bennett Field for The Irishman, Gearty chased long idles and material an editor can cut, and checked backgrounds for anachronism—a 1950s muffler sounds nothing like a 1980s one.
summers-6352c9: On Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen, Summers found that heavy percussion under robot running-and-shooting sequences tends to become a cacophony. In other scenes the director chose to let the music drive, and the effects came down instead.
summers-97b511: On Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen, Summers mixed against the composer team’s high-quality orchestral mock-ups early, learning where the score was thick and where effects could embellish it. When the real cue arrived, it only brought more clarity and transparency.
ribicoff-b9daeb: In the Severance finale, when the camera lurches as Innie Mark searches for the missing baby, Ribicoff added low-end and sub-frequency tones in waves matched to the camera movement, playing in the holes of a wall-to-wall score for a stomach-turning anxiety.
ribicoff-686368: On Severance, since dialogue mixer Bob Chefalas was adding room ambience to the production tracks, Ribicoff handed him the Foley too, so the same space processing sat on both and they lived in one room.
rohde-273ca4: For Pandora, Rohde backed leaning arches over floating mountains because they seemed feasible. Engineering showed the arches were just as hard and costly. The cautious option isn’t automatically the cheap one; test it.
stoeckinger-1cb636: In John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum’s glass fights, Stoeckinger’s team kept glass from sounding edgy and brittle by recording breaks at a higher sample rate, then rolling off highs with multiband EQ and compression. Ernest’s jaw break was a Granny Smith apple crunch.
semanick-862fc0: For Mrs. Potato Head’s ghostly far-eye voice in Toy Story 3, Semanick copied her line, advanced it several frames, sent it to reverb, printed only the reverb return and reversed it so it preceded the dialogue. He then added delays and reverb to the original.
morgan-fde4f0: For First Man, Iatrou Morgan studied NASA mission audio for its technical terms and cadence. For Armstrong's famous moon-step words she used Revoice Pro to match Ryan Gosling's rhythm and cadence to Neil's, then took the static from the original and added it to make it near identical.
becker-8632b0: For Sound of Metal’s cochlear implant, Becker rejected robot voices and analog distortion as belonging to the wrong world, instead testing software that generated genuinely digital artifacts with their own harmonics and transient noise.
massey-edc7f2: Massey split Ford v Ferrari’s 25-minute Le Mans sequence into four chapters and watched it end to end repeatedly to sculpt peaks and valleys, so the intensity never became a wall of noise.
massey-f7716b: On Ford v Ferrari, the composers delivered stereo tracks of each instrument group; Massey premixed his own instrument stems so he could push or pull specific parts against the cars.
hayes-167a61: On Les Misérables, for singers with huge dynamic range, such as Hugh Jackman and Russell Crowe, Hayes put two lavs on each actor: one close to the mouth for quiet passages and one lower down to take the loud ones.
johnson-8fa02a: For Alice in Wonderland’s 3D version Johnson pushed elements, even dialogue, into the surrounds and panned dialogue to the speaker’s position in frame. The same moves proved distracting in 2D, which got much less dialogue panning.
stateman-856908: On Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood, Stateman used what he calls rapid prototyping: an editor embedded in the cutting room gets near-final sound and dramatic intent working in the Avid mix during the editor’s cut, instead of temp placeholders.
stateman-3494e7: On Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood, with most of the music in hand early, Stateman could hear where the gaps were, carving acoustic space so dialogue sits front and centre and effects work around it — on Rick’s hero walk, fence rails and a distant whinny land on the beat.
rohde-51794d: Model-shop carvers working on Animal Kingdom’s Tree of Life proposed sculpting animals in relief instead of Rohde’s timid incised lines. He feared the cost; they knew their craft and assured him the difference was negligible. Trust specialists on what their own craft costs.
whitehead-cb7e5a: Whitehead’s first District 9 alien-tech palette, built partly from hydraulics and servos recorded at a New Zealand Air Force base, was classic blockbuster sci-fi. Neill Blomkamp wanted it far grungier and more real: real-world sounds with an alien core, so Whitehead started a new palette.
whitehead-c891cc: Because Neill Blomkamp described District 9’s aliens as insect-like with a hive-like society, Whitehead recorded as many insects as he could. He built a little insect recording booth and recorded bumblebees at 192kHz, finding interesting textures through micro recording.
whittle-ba29ea: Yates Whittle on a lesson from James Cameron on the Avatar films: to make a place feel quiet, you have to hear something small sound loud. In the forest, a foliage snap louder than you’d expect tells you how quiet it really is.
aadahl-9ab631: Aadahl warns against over-layering: every layer you add to a sound can strip the first sound of its power, essence and simplicity. The most potent sound is a single perfect sound against silence; like mixing too many paint colours, too many layers turn brown.
aadahl-c8118d: To fight ‘Too Much Sound’ on the final mix, Aadahl looks for what to remove: if an explosion lacks punch, perhaps the whoosh leading into it should cut out earlier to leave a beat of silence; in a car chase the backgrounds might be dropped entirely if they only add a wash.
stoeckinger-b784e9: Stoeckinger on the guns of John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum, built by sound designer Alan Rankin: layer a boomy, soft-attack layer with a sharp-attack one, covering the high and low ranges but not the mid-range. On assault rifles, the ping of the forcefully ejected shell is a dominant sound.
minto-009afd: On Battlefield 4, Minto’s team at DICE extended their systems to handle events near the player and then on them: a water sprinkler changes sound when you stand under it, adding a ‘water on helmet’ sound to make it personal.
deenen-e3c325: During mixes, Deenen runs every sound effect with hiss or noise through iZotope RX in real time, cutting noise by 3–8 dB to keep mixes clean and punchy. On Call of Duty: Ghosts, Ozone’s Matching EQ was his starting point for matching foreign-language dialogue to the English mix.
andersen-b0d185: For Inside, Andersen played synthesized sounds through a human skull and recorded them with contact mics. They initially came out sounding quite bad, so he post-processed them; the skull worked as a unique filter, boosting and dipping frequencies, giving a creepy, cold signature.
hayes-0fed81: Hayes matches the lav to the voice: a DPA 4071 for bass-heavy voices to curb low-end swell, and usually on the chest; a flatter 4061 for shriller voices and on heads or hats. On Guardians of the Galaxy, Bautista’s lav cable ran through his prosthetic scars, the mic poking out of one.
deenen-cf07fd: To find where an engine sounds best, Deenen places a wind-shielded lav in several spots on the car, repeating the same movement each time, and listens for build-ups of tone rather than noise. Too close to the exhaust gives lots of air movement but little tone.
bridgett-0826ac: Bridgett points to the new Army of Two: whenever the player gets behind cover, a subtle low-pass filter goes on some of the gun sounds so they feel more protected, and the filter comes off as soon as the cover disappears.
nelson-fa2773: Nelson finds that too many things around the room in the surrounds can be distracting, so he starts off fairly minimally and sits back to see what the screen needs. On The Book Thief that meant dubbing it simply and traditionally.
scarabosio-dd8e6c: For the quick cuts around the globe during the President's comet announcement in Don't Look Up, Scarabosio used hums and fans: a hum has tonality without being musical, so it could signal a change of location without feeling choppy.
deenen-cd5755: For Need for Speed cinematics, Deenen's team always started from real car recordings and enhanced them with other layers: in the early 2000s animals and metal, and by NFS Shift distortion and synth sweeteners.
sullivan-c6c716: With The Woman King rated PG-13 and little blood on camera, Sullivan's team let the soundtrack carry the violence. Prince-Bythewood wanted a deep, metallic, iron machete; Sullivan pulled a dark sound from her collection and gave each warrior's machete its own sound.
nair-a84125: On the trailer for Dharma, Nair based everything from the rain and thunder to the reverb tails on the trailer's tempo, so the effects sounded musical even though they were events.
nair-8486c1: For trailer effects, Nair avoids sounds heavy in the 2k-8k range: Dolby's LEQ meter weights 4k-8k peaks most, so the more peaks there, the faster the meter rises, and an approved trailer must stay within 85.
nair-7348f0: On the Dharma trailer, percussive elements set the tempo and energy, which let Nair drop sound elements rather than the score under dialogue; he says the mind won't notice and fills the gaps.
nair-501b15: For a bigger trailer sound, Nair uses more low-frequency elements, fewer mids and more in the surrounds, keeping the mix balanced rather than tilted to the rear. On the Dharma trailer he used multiband compression more than EQ for an even tone within the LEQ.
nielsen-85b556: Nielsen gets frustrated when a recordist brings back four identical door opens and closes. He wants a range from the same door: first soft, then loud, then rattled, kicked, pounded, slammed, and then the handle by itself.
nielsen-4eae32: For animal or creature vocals, Nielsen erases all the loud sounds from his work file and normalizes what's left: loud vocalizations tend to sound alike, while the very quiet ones you might otherwise discard have far more variety.
nielsen-a75bf5: Nielsen sends small pocket recorders out to people to record for him. People recording their own animals get more vocalizations, and more interesting ones, than a stranger pushing a large microphone into the animals' space would.
jerden-c25c4c: For a 'silent' dramatic moment in a trailer, Jerden still includes the sound effects but mixes them very low, running them through filters and delay, so that certain effects and dialogue ring out more prominently.
jerden-7b09c4: Jerden says silence in a trailer is such a strong statement that it must be well thought out and built into the trailer conceptually at the picture-editorial stage; done that way rather than as a cliché, it becomes a dramatic effect.
behlmer-c88fcd: Behlmer describes World War Z's car wreck, worked out collaboratively on the temp dub: after the impact a high-pitched tinnitus tone plays, everything goes silent, then the voices return muffled, grow clearer, and the sound bangs back to the outside world.
deenen-28674c: To fatten a sound, Deenen stacks two Renaissance Bass instances set to different frequencies, making both the sub and mid-range bigger. With the L1 limiter he plays with release: short releases create more distortion, longer ones smooth the sound out.
bridgett-3411fb: At Radical, Bridgett's team gave mixer snapshots three behaviors: one default snapshot sets group levels, multiplying ducking snapshots stack on top, and one override snapshot takes over for an event. Each channel or bus gets a maximum attenuation so simultaneous ducks can't over-attenuate.
bridgett-2769e8: Bridgett points out that game mixer snapshots needn't only change volume and panning: they can alter pitch, LFE send, 3D fall-off values, speaker assignment or listener position, so potentially any parameter of a sound or sound group can change.
massey-329bae: After No Time to Die's opening blast, James Harrison's effects lost their top end to sound underwater, so Massey put Zimmer's following music cue underwater too, using EQ and compression on certain instruments to hold a small dynamic window, then gradually opening the EQ to full fidelity.
albrechtsen-16eabd: Albrechtsen lends directors cheap handheld recorders to take on location so they listen for sounds, and asks crews never to shoot establishing shots mute, quietly picking up local ambiences instead. In a documentary ADR is not an option, so production sound must be as good as possible.
burtt-c42f35: For Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull's magnetic and telekinetic effects, Burtt recorded a buzzing mercury-vapor lamp in the Skywalker parking lot, slowed it down, played it backwards and put it all over his keyboard.
rydstrom-9b21ac: On West Side Story, Rydstrom treated the ambient sounds, from horns and sirens to pedestrians and crying babies, as their own kind of music, choosing and controlling each moment, such as when a construction truck or tire squeal is heard, for its rhythm and pitch.
whitehead-10b916: Whitehead used RX Spectral Repair to remove birds and insects from many recordings on The Hobbit. He also declicks fire recordings to keep the warm roar without the crackles, and dereverbs good indoor recordings so they can work on exterior scenes.
becker-96bd66: To capture Ruben's internal sounds in Sound of Metal, Becker placed a super-sensitive mic on Riz Ahmed's chest for his breathing and blood pressure, a tiny mic inside his mouth, and a geophone on his scalp to capture low-frequency vibration.
lee-b89ce0: As First Man's picture editor Tom Cross began cutting, Lee's team sent him a kit of sounds (turbulence, shake, helmet and glove clicks) so he could weave those textures into his cut early on.
klyce-5a461b: In The Killer's closing-kitchen scene, Fincher wanted the room busy, then slowly quieter; Klyce's team punctuated the quiet with the kitchen door swinging open on staff laughing, cleaning and playing music, what Klyce calls the escape hatch of her fear.
andersen-34b6d8: Andersen sometimes applies the spectral blueprints of traditional instruments to non-instrumental sounds using convolution and match-EQ, using the orchestra's spectral makeup as a frame of reference when composing electroacoustic soundscapes for games like Inside and Control.
lievsay-66d5e0: For I Am Legend's emptied New York, research by director Francis Lawrence pictured the city reverting to nature, like a New England forest. Lievsay says gathering those sounds was easier than removing traffic and city sounds from production recordings; some scenes had to be replaced with ADR.
becker-a80d3a: On Sound of Metal, Becker recorded with a very large omni mic plus, at times, close-up mics. He gave editor Mikkel one stereo recording, then after the edit re-conformed to the other mics, so the same recording could zoom from a massive sound to something very precise.
myers-4e0928: On Tokyo DisneySea's Nemo & Friends SeaRider, Myers's team first set up the expectation of a submarine, then, once guests are 'shrunk' and underwater, removed all the submarine sound effects so audiences feel they are floating and interacting with the characters.
wood-b8dd1b: Wood's Star Wars loop group are improvisers who know every film reference and speak Huttese and Jawa, because the whole movie gets covered in a couple of days. Their lines must sound authentic without pulling focus, like two stormtroopers' improvised hallway chatter on Starkiller Base in The Force Awakens.
allen-1026e2: On Parenthood, Allen chooses wire placement after watching rehearsal for physical business, such as hugging, carrying a bag or talking to the right in a car.
